When President John F. Kennedy’s body arrived at Bethesda Naval Hospital on November 22, 1963, the official story seemed straightforward: he had been transported from Dallas in the ornate bronze casket seen by millions on television beside Jacqueline Kennedy.
But multiple witnesses later claimed something didn’t add up.
Bethesda autopsy technician Paul O’Connor stated that JFK’s body arrived not in the famous bronze casket, but inside a “cheap gray shipping casket.” Researcher David Lifton later argued that records and witness testimony suggested Kennedy’s body may have secretly arrived earlier than the official motorcade — raising disturbing questions about what happened before the autopsy began.
Dennis David, a member of the Bethesda staff, claimed he witnessed a black hearse delivering a shipping casket carrying Kennedy’s body well before Jackie Kennedy and the ceremonial bronze casket arrived. Others involved in the autopsy, including Jim Jenkins, also recalled the body arriving in a simple transport container and body bag rather than the casket publicly associated with the President.
These accounts fueled one of the darkest and most controversial theories surrounding the JFK assassination: that Kennedy’s body may have been secretly altered before the official autopsy in order to change or obscure ballistic evidence.
Supporters of the theory point to conflicting autopsy notes, witness discrepancies, and questions surrounding the chain of custody. Critics argue that memories decades later are unreliable and that confusion during the chaotic aftermath of the assassination explains the contradictions.
More than 60 years later, the alleged “shipping casket” remains one of the most haunting mysteries connected to the Kennedy assassination — a detail that continues to divide researchers, historians, and conspiracy investigators alike.

posts.text:
Suppose you get a 2 billion line of code (LoC) Lean proof of the Riemann Hypothesis or the Collatz Conjecture. What have you actually learned?

The proof of Fermat’s Last Theorem is ~13M LoC in Lean, but at least there’s a human-readable mathematical spine underpinning it: Wiles/Taylor-Wiles, and you can follow the argument end to end. 

A kernel-verified proof with no human-compressible argument feels like it could be a genuinely different object: proof without understanding.

What happens when the shortest known proof certificate is machine-scale, but the shortest known explanation is nonexistent?

TRUE

New FBI special agents and intelligence analysts must visit the U.S. Holocaust Memorial Museum during Academy training (part of the ethics curriculum since ~2000). Official FBI site confirms it remains required. It's a post-selection training step, not a pre-hire condition, but trainees who fail to complete it do not become agents.
